name: Tree of Thoughts
what: Having the model explore several reasoning branches, evaluate which are promising, and backtrack from dead ends, search instead of a single chain.
mechanism: Chain-of-thought commits to one path; if step two is wrong, everything after it inherits the error. Tree of Thoughts reframes problem solving as search: generate several candidate next steps, have the model evaluate which look promising, expand the best ones, and abandon dead ends, breadth-first or depth-first over partial solutions. Yao and colleagues showed the payoff on tasks where first ideas usually fail, most famously the Game of 24, where chain-of-thought solved a small fraction and tree search solved most. The cost is structural: you are running many generations and evaluations per problem plus orchestration code. Reasoning models with extended thinking now do a version of explore-and-backtrack internally, which is why explicit tree scaffolding today is mostly reserved for problems with a checkable notion of a good partial step.
when_works: Puzzles, planning, and constrained problems where early choices determine success and single-chain reasoning walks into dead ends, the original paper's Game of 24 results are dramatic.
when_fails: Everyday tasks: it multiplies cost and latency by the branch count, and reasoning models with extended thinking now do much of this internally without the scaffolding.
how: Prompt the model to propose 3 next steps, rate each for promise, expand the best, and repeat. In practice this needs orchestration code or an agent framework rather than a single prompt.

examples.label: Generate, score, prune, expand
examples.prompt: Problem: {HARD_PROBLEM}. Step 1: propose 4 genuinely different first moves. Step 2: for each, rate 1-10 how likely it leads to a full solution, one sentence of justification each. Step 3: take the highest-rated move, propose 3 continuations, rate those. Step 4: if the best path stalls, back up to the second-rated first move and repeat.
examples.note: One prompt cannot truly search, but this compressed version of the ToT loop already beats committing to the first idea on puzzle-like problems.

examples.label: The everyday variant, brainstorm then prune
examples.prompt: Give 8 distinct approaches to {PROBLEM}, one line each, no elaboration. Then evaluate all 8 against these criteria: {COST, TIME, RISK}. Then fully develop only the top 2 and state why the other 6 lost.
examples.note: Separating generation from evaluation is the reusable core of tree of thoughts; most tasks need only one level of the tree.

faq.q: When is tree of thoughts worth the cost?
faq.a: When first attempts usually fail and partial progress is checkable: puzzles, constrained planning, search-like configuration problems. For everyday work, generate-then-prune captures most of the value in one prompt.
Largely, for reasoning models: internal deliberation explores and backtracks without external scaffolding. Explicit trees remain useful when you need the search visible and steerable.

faq.q: What makes a good evaluation step?
faq.a: A checkable definition of promising. If the model cannot score a partial solution better than chance, the tree degenerates into an expensive random walk.

paper: Yao et al., Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models (2023)
